title: Sporadic Hemiplegic Migraine with Seizures and Transient MRI Abnormalities
case_prompt:
A 24-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 2-hour history of left-sided throbbing headache associated with blurred vision, followed by development of right-sided hemiparesis and aphasia. Shortly thereafter, she experienced right focal motor seizures. 

Her past medical history dated back 12 years, when she had her first episode of unilateral throbbing headache with nausea and occasional photophobia, followed by transient hemiparesis (alternating sides) lasting a few hours, with spontaneous full recovery. Prior investigations during those episodes—including head CT, brain MRI, angiography, serum and CSF lactate, and other biochemical tests—had been normal. There was no family history of similar events, and connective tissue disease had been ruled out. She had been treated first with flunarizine and later with topiramate but continued to have one or two attacks per month.

On examination during this admission, she was alert and cooperative but had motor aphasia and right-sided weakness with normal sensation. Funduscopic and other systemic examinations were unremarkable. 

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.7 g/dL, WBC 6.0×10^9/L, platelets 223×10^9/L, normal metabolic panel, normal thyroid function tests, normal serum and CSF lactate, and negative ANA, anti–double-stranded DNA, anticardiolipin antibodies, antiphospholipid antibodies, and beta-2 glycoprotein. EEG showed no hemispheric dysfunction.

Brain MRI demonstrated diffuse cortical swelling and mild cortical hyperintensity of the left hemisphere on T2-weighted and FLAIR images. Diffusion-weighted images were normal. T1-weighted images, MR angiography, and postcontrast studies showed no abnormalities.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Acute brain infarction was considered but ruled out — “Diffusion-weighted images were normal enabling us to rule out an acute brain infarction.”  
2. Intracranial neoplasm or infection was considered but excluded — “There was no tumor, obvious lesion, or sign of infection, such as abscess or encephalitis, on MR images.”  
3. Epilepsy with postictal (Todd’s) paralysis was considered but EEG was normal — “EEG showed no hemispheric dysfunction.”  
4. Metabolic and mitochondrial disorders were considered but lactate and biochemical parameters were normal — “CSF lactate was also normal along with serum lactate... other biochemical parameters were normal.”  
5. Autoimmune and antiphospholipid syndromes were considered but serologies were negative — “ANA, anti-DNA negative, ACLA, APL, Beta 2 glycoprotein negative.”  
6. Familial hemiplegic migraine was considered but family history was absent — “Since there was no family history, she was diagnosed as having sporadic hemiplegic migraine.”  
7. Migralepsy (seizure triggered by migraine aura) was considered but the reversible MRI changes and clinical course favored hemiplegic migraine — “The possibility that transient brain MRI abnormalities in a patient with migraine with aura followed by seizures may be due to migralepsy should be borne in mind to avoid misdiagnosis and potentially aggressive procedures.”
